title: A Dead Star Spins Every 8 Minutes and Sends Mystery Radio Signals
summary:
Astronomers have traced strange radio signals to two stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth. One is a dead star spinning once every eight minutes, and the other looks a lot like our Sun.

Researchers at Curtin University's International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) made the discovery. The pair, called GPM J071507-114153, holds a white dwarf and a G-type star circling each other. A white dwarf is the dense leftover of a star that burned through its fuel.

Until now, such pulses had only been seen with a smaller, cooler red dwarf star. This is the first time they have been found with a Sun-like companion.

The pair belongs to a rare group called long-period transients, or LPTs, which send out radio signals that appear and vanish. Only about a dozen have been seen since the first was found in 2021.

The team studied more than 100 hours of radio observations, which also showed magnetic storms on the Sun-like star. Dr. Sam McSweeney said it is amazing that radio waves can reveal storms on a star so far away.
why_it_matters: Studying faraway stars shows you how scientists solve mysteries using clues they cannot even see, just like a detective.

background_read: Stars send out radio waves that telescopes on Earth can pick up, and astronomers study these waves to learn about faraway stars.
A white dwarf is what is left of a star after it has burned through its fuel, and it can spin as it circles another star.
Some pairs of stars send out radio pulses that appear and vanish, and finding a new kind of pair helps scientists understand how these strange signals work.
